hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Berberine lowers LDL cholesterol in randomized trials. I'm interested in how that connects to ApoB, artery plaque, and the gut microbiome.

A meta-analysis pooling 14 placebo-controlled trials found an average LDL reduction of approximately 18 mg/dL.

Recent randomized-trial evidence also found reductions in ApoB, which estimates the number of circulating particles that can contribute to atherosclerosis.

Early clinical evidence also suggests berberine can reduce plaque in the arteries. And at least one of those studies also found a modest reduction in TMAO, a metabolite linked to gut microbial metabolism and implicated in atherosclerosis. 

One interesting detail from the newer research: ApoB decreased in both men and women, with a larger response in women.

In a new placebo-controlled trial in women, berberine lowered ApoB by about 13 mg/dL relative to placebo. Researchers compared those results with an earlier trial in men and found evidence suggesting women had a stronger lipid response.

What is interesting is that this may just be a dose-dependent effect. In a separate study, women had almost three times the blood exposure to berberine after the same dose.

Together, these findings make berberine a promising compound for cardiovascular health, with potential benefits spanning lipid metabolism, artery health, and the gut microbiome.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick on berberine, a plant compound sold as a supplement. She says a pooled look at 14 placebo-controlled trials found it lowered LDL cholesterol by about 18 mg/dL on average, newer trials found drops in ApoB (the count of particles that can clog arteries), and early studies suggest it may reduce artery plaque. The effect looked stronger in women, possibly because they absorb more from the same dose.

She calls it promising for heart health. Promising, not a cure.

If your cholesterol's up, it's worth a yarn with your GP. Don't swap or stop any heart meds for a supplement without them, and tell them about anything you take.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
The Man Who Stopped Eating for More Than a Year—and Still Died Young
Imagine being so tired of carrying extra weight that you decide to stop eating completely. Not for a few days. Not for a few weeks. For more than an entire year. That is exactly what a young Scottish man named Angus Barbieri did in the 1960s. His story is one of the most extreme weight-loss journeys ever recorded, and it still raises big questions today.
In 1965, Angus was 27 years old and weighed about 456 pounds. He worked at his father’s fish-and-chip shop and struggled with food. He walked into a hospital in Dundee, Scotland, and asked the doctors to help him fast. They expected it would last only a short time, maybe a few weeks. Instead, Angus kept going. For 382 days he ate no solid food at all. He drank tea, coffee, and sparkling water, and he took vitamins and other supplements the doctors gave him. Medical staff checked him often to make sure he stayed safe.
By the time he stopped in July 1966, he weighed just 180 pounds. He had lost more than 270 pounds. He broke his fast with a simple boiled egg and a piece of bread with butter. He told reporters he had almost forgotten what food tasted like, but he enjoyed the meal. Over the next years he kept most of the weight off. He moved, got married, and had two sons. Photos from that time show a completely different man from the one who started the fast.
But the story does not end with lasting thinness. Angus died in September 1990 at only 51 years old after a short illness. He had succeeded at one of the hardest weight-loss challenges anyone has ever tried, and he stayed near his lower weight for the rest of his life. Still, he did not reach old age. Doctors today strongly warn that long fasts like his are dangerous and should never be tried without full medical care. Angus’s record still stands as the longest documented fast without solid food, but his early death shows that dropping a huge amount of weight is not the same as living a long, healthy life.
hits.draft_en:
Shawn Baker tells the story of Angus Barbieri, a 27-year-old Scotsman who weighed about 456 pounds in 1965 and fasted for 382 days under hospital watch, on just tea, coffee, sparkling water and vitamins. He dropped to 180 pounds and kept most of it off. But he died in 1990 at only 51.

Baker's point: losing a huge amount of weight isn't the same as living a long, healthy life. And doctors warn long fasts like that should never be tried without full medical care.

Crash efforts make headlines. What keeps you going is the boring stuff: decent food, moving every day, and regular checks with your GP.

Higher body fat is a better predictor of testosterone than age.

Chronological age alone explained just 2.5% of the variation in total testosterone in men aged 20 to 59. Including measures of body fat, visceral fat, or waist circumference increased that to roughly 18-20%.

And a simple waist measurement performed about as well as DXA-derived visceral fat for explaining differences in testosterone levels.

A tape measure (something you can use at home) captured much of the same information as advanced imaging!

This is one reason I talk so much about visceral fat (the fat surrounding your organs). Excess visceral fat can promote inflammation and insulin resistance, both of which can interfere with testosterone regulation. Fat tissue also contains aromatase, an enzyme that converts testosterone into estradiol, a form of estrogen.

The relationship can run both ways - lower testosterone can favor fat accumulation, creating a feedback loop.

These are observational data, but they suggest some of what gets labeled “age-related” low testosterone may be more closely tied to body composition.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
Imagine a doctor who spends his life checking other scientists’ work—like a detective for research—and discovers that a huge amount of what we “know” about food and health is shaky or just plain wrong. That’s John Ioannidis.

John Ioannidis is one of the most respected scientists in the world. He is a professor of medicine and statistics at Stanford University. His famous 2005 paper, “Why Most Published Research Findings Are False,” has been read millions of times and changed how people think about science. He studies how research is done and why so many studies turn out to be wrong. Scientists and journals listen to him carefully.

When he looked at nutritional epidemiology—the science that tries to figure out which foods help or hurt us by watching large groups of people—he said the field is in serious trouble and needs a big fix.
Here’s what he found, in plain language:
Most of these studies just ask people what they remember eating and then look for links to diseases. Almost every food ends up looking “significant.” That leads to crazy claims if you take the numbers at face value. For example, the math can suggest that eating 12 hazelnuts a day adds 12 years to your life, or that two slices of bacon a day shortens your life by a decade (worse than smoking). 

Ioannidis says those results are almost certainly not real. They mostly show bias, errors in how people report their diets, and other problems that create noise instead of truth.

He argues that small differences in ordinary foods rarely cause big changes in how long people live or whether they get major diseases. Extreme problems (like not getting enough of a vitamin, or eating way too many calories) matter. Everyday variations usually do not.

Ioannidis has said the field has largely become a “null field”—meaning most of the single-food or single-nutrient findings are probably zero or close to zero once you account for biases. He has even said nutritional epidemiology has “grown old and died” and that researchers should stop producing more of the same observational studies and move to better methods, especially large, carefully done randomized trials where people are actually assigned different diets.

In short: He respects the hard work of people in the field but believes the main tools they have used for decades produce mostly unreliable results. That is why headlines about one food being a miracle or a poison keep changing—and why he says the science needs radical reform.
His warnings matter because he is not an outsider. He is a top expert who has spent decades showing how science can go wrong, and many other researchers take his critiques seriously even when they disagree with parts of them.
hits.draft_en:
Shawn Baker on John Ioannidis, the Stanford professor famous for his paper "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False". Baker says Ioannidis looked hard at food-and-health studies and found most of them just ask people what they remember eating, then hunt for links to disease. Taken at face value, the maths can claim 12 hazelnuts a day adds 12 years to your life, or two slices of bacon takes a decade off.

Ioannidis says results like those are almost certainly not real. Small everyday food choices rarely make big differences. The big stuff does: not enough of a key nutrient, or way too many calories.

That's why the headlines flip every year. Don't chase them. Eat real food, not too much, keep moving.

When scientists measured stomach acid, humans came out with the lowest pH of the three. In one careful study, fasting human stomachs averaged about 1.1, while dogs averaged 1.8. Wolves are estimated around 1–2, but the data on them is limited. Humans consistently show the most acidic stomachs among these animals.
That very low pH is not random. It is the perfect environment for digesting protein. At a pH of about 1.5 to 2, stomach acid does two big jobs. First, it unfolds proteins so they are easier to break apart. Second, it turns the inactive enzyme pepsinogen into active pepsin. Pepsin then cuts the long protein chains into smaller pieces. This works especially well on the proteins found in meat, eggs, and dairy.
Dogs and wolves handle meat fine, but their stomach acid is often less consistently low than ours. Human stomachs stay powerfully acidic in the fasting state and are optimized for the kind of protein digestion that happens when you eat animal foods. The same acid also kills many bacteria that can ride along with food.
In short, the lowest pH stomach acid is best for digesting proteins — and humans have some of the lowest among dogs, wolves, and people. That is not an accident of evolution. It is a digestive system ready for meat.

Meds can quiet the worst noises, yet they often leave people overweight, foggy, and still battling voices or flat feelings. Researchers took people with schizophrenia-spectrum or bipolar-1 disorders and randomly assigned them to a ketogenic diet or their usual diet for one month. Then many stayed on keto for a total of four months. They checked blood ketones every day to make sure people were actually in ketosis.

Positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), negative symptoms (flat mood, low drive), depression scores, and thinking skills all improved sharply—statistically solid results. Higher ketone levels lined up with better mood and better metabolic numbers, even after accounting for weight loss. In other words, the ketones themselves seemed to help the brain, not just the bathroom scale.

This was not a miracle cure and people stayed on their regular meds. Still, it is the first solid controlled evidence that a high-fat, very-low-carb way of eating can fix the metabolic mess that so often rides along with psychosis and, at the same time, lighten the psychiatric load. •  This was linked to more fiber-fermenting gut bacteria producing gas (mostly odorless hydrogen, methane, and CO₂) plus short-chain fatty acids.

The study’s abstract notes higher numbers of anal gas evacuations, more flatulence sensations, larger post-meal gas volume, and larger colonic content on the Mediterranean diet, with substantial shifts in microbial metabolism despite smaller changes in overall microbiota composition.

Bones dug up across North America tell a surprising story about the first farmers. Long before Europeans arrived, people who hunted and gathered wild foods left behind skeletons that were often taller and healthier than those of the early farmers who followed them.
Scientists have compared thousands of ancient skeletons from sites in the eastern United States, the Southwest, and other regions. Hunter-gatherers usually had longer bones, meaning they grew taller. Their teeth showed far fewer cavities. Signs of childhood stress and poor nutrition, such as porous bones in the skull that point to anemia, were also less common. When groups switched to growing corn and other crops, many of those health markers got worse. People became shorter on average. Tooth decay jumped because the new diet was heavy in starchy foods that stuck to teeth. More skeletons showed evidence of infection and nutritional shortfalls.
The change did not happen overnight, and not every group suffered equally. Some communities adapted better than others, and later farming societies sometimes recovered some of the lost height once they added more variety to their meals. Still, the overall pattern from the bones is clear. Relying more on crops and living in denser villages brought new problems that the older hunting-and-gathering way of life had largely avoided. Population numbers rose with farming, but individual health often declined for a time.
These findings come from careful study of real skeletal remains, not just theories. They show that the move to agriculture was a trade-off: more food in good years, but greater risk of disease and weaker bodies for many people.

There are essential fatty acids and essential amino acids. There is no essential carbohydrate.

The body does need some glucose, mainly for red blood cells, which have no mitochondria. But the liver and kidneys can make all of it through gluconeogenesis, typically around 100 to 150 grams a day in adults, using lactate, glycerol from fat, and a small amount of amino acids.

Carb tolerance still varies a lot from person to person, and my new book, The Carb Crisis, explains why. The evidence is clear: carbs are optional, not required. Preorder link in the first reply.

hits.name: Ken D Berry MD
hits.text:
Two researchers opened a cookbook, picked 50 ordinary ingredients, and checked the medical journals to see how many had been studied for a link to cancer.

Forty of the 50 had. And the results are a mess.

They found 264 study results, and 191 said the food raised or lowered cancer risk.

But three out of four of those estimates had weak statistical support or none at all. When the bigger pooled studies looked at the same foods, the average effect was about zero.

One of those researchers was John Ioannidis of Stanford, who wrote "Why Most Published Research Findings Are False."

In 2018 he wrote in JAMA that nutrition research "needs radical reform."

He also showed what those headline numbers say if you take them literally:

12 hazelnuts a day adds 12 years of life.
3 cups of coffee adds about 12 more.
1 egg a day costs you 6 years.
2 slices of bacon a day costs a decade, worse than smoking.

He was making a point. That math is silly.

So when a scary food headline pops up, ask four questions:

1. Was it observational? A link isn't proof.
2. How did they know what people ate? Usually they just asked.
3. Is it a relative risk? 20% more of a tiny risk is still tiny.
4. Did a real trial ever test it?

Beta carotene is the classic example. In observational studies, people with the highest blood levels had a 31% lower risk of dying.

When large trials actually gave people beta carotene, they ruled out even a small benefit.

The best experiment is the one you run on yourself. Change how you eat, then watch your labs and the scale over months.

Doctor: I’d like to start you on a low-dose daily medication for your chronic condition. The data show it reduces long-term risk, and once we start, the plan is usually lifelong—stopping can reverse the benefit.
Patient: I’m not comfortable committing to a drug for life. I don’t trust the companies that make these drugs. They routinely misrepresent their own studies, hide unfavorable data, and simply don’t publish negative trials. When a researcher produces results they don’t like, funding disappears.
Doctor: Most trials are registered now, and we have more transparency than we used to. The agencies do require disclosure of certain results.
Patient: That’s not what the record shows. Companies have been caught suppressing negative studies and spinning the ones they do publish. And it isn’t just the companies—the medical journals themselves have authors who’ve documented how industry money distorts the literature. Multiple senior academics have written that pharmaceutical funding has corrupted large parts of academic research.
Doctor: There are conflicts of interest, I agree, but the peer-review process and independent analyses still catch a lot of problems.
Patient: The same companies also dominate the advertising that keeps the major news outlets afloat. When the bulk of your revenue comes from drug ads, critical coverage of those same drugs becomes rare. That’s not a conspiracy theory; it’s how the business model works.
Doctor: News organizations do have conflicts, but they also report negative stories when they surface.
Patient: Then there’s the FDA. The revolving door is well documented—regulators leave government and go straight into industry jobs, and industry people move into regulatory roles. That’s classic regulatory capture. Public-private partnerships and intellectual-property deals have created similar conflicts at the NIH. The people who are supposed to be independent watchdogs have financial ties to the companies they’re regulating.
Doctor: Those arrangements are meant to accelerate research. There are ethics rules and disclosure requirements.
Patient: The rules haven’t stopped repeated cases of fraud. Companies have been caught faking data, off-label promotion, and concealing risks. The usual outcome is a fine that is a fraction of the revenue the drug generated. No one goes to jail, and the same companies continue selling the products. That pattern has repeated for decades.
Doctor: I… those settlements do happen, and the penalties are often small relative to profits. I don’t have a strong answer for that.
Patient: So given all of that—hidden negative data, journal corruption, advertising control of the press, regulatory capture at the FDA and NIH, and fraud settled with wrist-slap fines—why should I trust that this particular lifelong medication is safe and necessary rather than simply profitable?
Doctor: (quietly) Those are real problems. I don’t have a good rebuttal to the pattern you’ve described. The system has been compromised in the ways you said. I still think the drug might help in your case based on the published data, but I understand why that data doesn’t look reliable to you. We can hold off if you’d rather not start it.
